# Generator shortcut answer

The strongest plausible rival that fits every canonical demonstration is **merge disconnected components of the same color before building the output strip**. The public pairs never reuse one color on two disconnected objects, so they cannot distinguish per-object counting from per-color counting.

An exact generated counterexample is below (`seed=41000`, `sample_index=30`, `difficulty=medium`, `scene_profile=compact_5x5_three`):

```text
0 7 0 0 6
7 7 0 0 0
0 0 6 6 0
0 0 6 6 0
0 0 6 0 0
```

It contains three 4-connected objects: color 6 of size 5, color 7 of size 3, and a disconnected color 6 singleton. The intended per-object rule returns:

```text
6 6 6 6 6 0 7 7 7 0 6
```

The rival first merges both color-6 objects and instead returns:

```text
6 6 6 6 6 6 0 7 7 7
```

I checked the intended output by applying the canonical Racket `program_solution` through the persistent repository runner; it exactly matched the independent Python mirror. The source-bound record, including the input, both outputs, generator SHA-256, and canonical-program SHA-256, is `checks/shortcut_counterexample.json`.

Yes, version 5 emits these cases deliberately. `sample_index % 3 == 0` selects `split_color_witness`. The high-power probe used the semantic gate's pinned sampler for 100 lessons in each of easy, medium, and hard. This rival disagreed on one demonstration in every lesson—300/300 lesson-level refutations—and survived zero demonstration sets (`checks/lesson_probe_300.json`). The same three-step schedule also emits an equal-size/different-color witness to refute the secondary rival that ignores or reverses the ascending-color tie-break.
